Why practices run ScamPrep

One convincing phone call can undo a decade of careful planning. The fallout lands on the practice, not just the client.

  • Keep the assets through the wealth transfer

    When assets pass on to heirs, the financial advisor usually doesn't. The Resilience Report puts your name in front of clients' adult children every month, associated with good news about their parent.

  • A scam is an AUM event

    More than twelve thousand people each lost $100k+ to fraud in 2025 — and that's just what was reported. Those are withdrawals no portfolio plans for, and sometimes the greater cost is the family conversation after. Trained clients lower the odds of both.

  • Differentiation that takes one sentence

    “We train our clients against scams — and show their families the progress.” No rate table, model portfolio, or planning tool says that.

  • Fewer fire drills of the bad kind

    Talking clients out of scams, or supporting them through the fallout, can take days or weeks. Trained clients spare your practice those unforeseen costs.

Preventing a single loss pays for years of the program.

Sources: FBI IC3 2025 Internet Crime Report · Cerulli Associates, on the great wealth transfer and heir retention

The deliverable

A monthly report with your name on it

Every month, the family members each client chooses receive a one-page Resilience Report — what was practiced, what was caught, what's being reinforced next — co-branded to your firm.

Monitoring tools message families when something bad may have happened. This is the opposite: recurring proof that their parent is getting harder to fool. It arrives with your name on it, in the inboxes of the generation that inherits. Your practice sees the aggregate view: participation, catch rates, and who might need a closer look.

Questions advisors ask

How will my clients react?

Better than you'd guess. Framing does the work, and you control it. This is the same simulate-and-coach training Fortune 500 firms require of every employee, including the CEO. It's offered as a benefit, never an accusation: every participant opts in personally, drills are gentle, and coaching is private. Sharp clients tend to enjoy catching them.

What will our compliance team ask?

The usual questions have short answers:

  • Account access: none — ScamPrep never touches money, accounts, or credentials.
  • Integrations and data feeds: none.
  • Data held: the contact channels a participant consents to — nothing financial.
  • Texts and calls: only with written consent, per the TCPA. Enrollment starts with email.

There's very little surface to review.

What happens when a client misses a drill?

A private, 30-second, friendly lesson in the moment — no shame, no public score. The family sees the month's trend, not a gotcha log, and you see aggregates. The design follows published research on older-adult learning: positive framing, immediate reassurance, never fear.

Where does this sit with the Senior Safe Act and trusted-contact rules?

ScamPrep is not a compliance product and doesn't claim to satisfy any rule. But the regulatory direction is clear: the Senior Safe Act protects firms that train and report, and trusted-contact rules push firms to engage families before there's a problem. A prevention program with monthly family touchpoints is exactly that posture, documented.
